issue_context.title: Two modbus slaves are blocking Home Assistant from wrapping up the start up phase
issue_context.body:
### The problem

I have seen several issues titled "Something is blocking Home Assistant from wrapping up the start up phase", but none of them seem to have been followed up or solved. In my case the problem shows up when I add a second slave. I have two SDM630 kWh meters on a [RS232/RS485 to Ethernet Converter](https://www.waveshare.com/product/iot-communication/wired-comm-converter/ethernet-to-rs232-rs485/rs232-485-to-eth.htm). All sensors for both slaves are the same, only different in name and slave number:

    - name: SDM630 Phase 1 line to neutral volts
      slave: 1
      address: 0
      input_type: input
      count: 2
      precision: 2
      data_type: float32
      unit_of_measurement: V
      device_class: voltage
      state_class: measurement

... and a lot of other slave 1 sensors. Same for slave 2, which I have named SDM631:

    - name: SDM631 Phase 1 line to neutral volts
      slave: 2
      address: 0
      input_type: input
      count: 2
      precision: 2
      data_type: float32
      unit_of_measurement: V
      device_class: voltage
      state_class: measurement

When I remove all slave 2 sensors from the yaml, Home Assistant starts up fine. The same when I remove all slave 1 sensors. Only when I use slave 1 and slave 2 sensors together the blocking warning appears. It takes 15 minutes for Home Assistant to start up (shutdown is also very slow). After Home Assistant continues, every sensor of both slaves is present, active and updated nicely.

Any idea if this is a bug in the modbus code or could there be another cause?


### What version of Home Assistant Core has the issue?

2023.1.7

### What was the last working version of Home Assistant Core?

_No response_

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant Container

### Integration causing the issue

modbus

### Link to integration documentation on our website

https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/modbus/

### Diagnostics information

_No response_

### Example YAML snippet

```yaml
modbus:
  - name: Waveshare Meterkast
    type: tcp
    host: !secret modbus_ip1
    port: !secret modbus_port1
    delay: 1
    retry_on_empty: true
    message_wait_milliseconds: 200
    sensors: !include sensors_sdm630_min.yaml
```


### Anything in the logs that might be useful for us?

```txt
2023-01-30 19:20:38.009 ...
2023-01-30 19:34:10.770 WARNING (MainThread) [homeassistant.bootstrap] Setup timed out for bootstrap - moving forward
2023-01-30 19:34:25.781 WARNING (MainThread) [homeassistant.core] Something is blocking Home Assistant from wrapping up the start up phase. We're going to continue anyway. Please report the following info at https://github.com/home-assistant/core/issues: [long list of all integrations]
```


### Additional information

_No response_

please run the modbus integration with debug as pr documentation, so that we can see what happens.

You need to run 2 tests:
a) only have slave 1 configured
b) only have slave 2 configured

I suspect you will see startup problems in b), and most likely because slave 2 do not respond.

The modbus code do not know about slave 1 and 2, that is just part of a common address (slave + address) so I have no idea where the modbus code should fail. However your ethernet/rs485 typically knows about the slaves and of course so  do your devices. If slave 2 do not respond then you will have a startup problem.

Something blocking the startup phase is a very common problem and relates not only to modbus but to a larger part of the integrations.

Do you run any custom component that uses modbus, if so, please deactivate them, modbus started using a new version of pymodbus in version 2023.1 and we have seen several “clashes” with custom components.

> Do you run any custom component that uses modbus,

No, but I do use HACS with some custom components. To be sure, I removed these and HACS completely and then performed some tests (next comment).

> You need to run 2 tests: a) only have slave 1 configured b) only have slave 2 configured
> 
> I suspect you will see startup problems in b), and most likely because slave 2 do not respond.

I really see no difference in starting up with only slave 1, only slave 2 or slave 1 and 2 together except for the delay in startup and the blocking message. A summary of the tests I performed with debugging enabled:

a) only slave 1 configured ([complete log here](https://github.com/jov58/home-assistant/blob/main/modbus/slave1-only.log))

... more of these messages (sometimes for 15 minutes, this time for 5 minutes) while desktop says 'Wrapping up ...'
... During this stage, I can already see entities of both slaves responding on the desktop.

> Something blocking the startup phase is a very common problem and relates not only to modbus but to a larger part of the integrations.

Personally this is my first, but it seems to be so, yes. Nevertheless, this is a case where we can switch the blocking problem on and off as we like. Perhaps that can help on narrowing down the problem. Since the blocking only appears when using two slaves and disappears when removing one of them. I can only conclude that this specific configuration triggers a problem somewhere. It could be a misty something in the modbus code or -through innocent modbus code- it could be something in Home Assistants' core code further up the road. I can imagine that something like this is not easy to find.

It would have been nice if Home Assistant could provide more info on that 'Something' that is blocking!

Are there any others things I could try or debug to get more info about this problem?

Looking at the logs supplied it is clear that you never receive anything from your devices. You see pymodbus SENDING but not RECEIVING...and then it retries etc...

Now why do 1 slave not make HA signal modbus is slow to start, that is actually quite simple, it depends on the number of configured sensors, too many sensors then the sum of timeout are bigger than HA likes.


You are using tcp, which by default use the socket framer, are you sure that is correct ? most cheap tcp - rs485 converters do not manipulate the messages, but simple pass them, that is why we have rtuovertcp.

Actually homeassisstant do tell you exactly when which integratations start, and lately it even includes the startup time in seconds....that is a lot more than "something".

We might consider changing modbus so that it starts fast and does the real work afterwards, right now connections need to be open and all sensors read once (initial state) before we consider modbus have started.

> Looking at the logs supplied it is clear that you never receive anything from your devices. You see pymodbus SENDING but not RECEIVING...and then it retries etc...

Yes, but I _am_ receiving. While I follow HA's log live in a PuTTY window and see all those SENDING messages filling the screen, I can see sensors from both slaves being updated in a HA browser window at the same time. The first already a few seconds after the first SENDING message. So, no RECEIVING message but still receiving data.

Even with as few as 5 sensors per slave I never see a RECEIVING message. In that case I see 10 SENDING messages, a little pause, 10 SENDING messages again etc. And I see HA updating at the same time. If pymodbus would be constantly retrying because it received no data, there would be no pause between series I think? And I imagine I wouldn't see HA updating if it didn't receive data. Are you sure there is nothing wrong with the RECEIVING message implementation?

> 
> Now why do 1 slave not make HA signal modbus is slow to start, that is actually quite simple, it depends on the number of configured sensors, too many sensors then the sum of timeout are bigger than HA likes.

I didn't realize that, so I immediately tried with 5 sensors per slave. That works, HA starts quickly and no blocking message.

> 
> You are using tcp, which by default use the socket framer, are you sure that is correct ? most cheap tcp - rs485 converters do not manipulate the messages, but simple pass them, that is why we have rtuovertcp.

Yes, I'm sure. According to the seller, [my converter even is an industrial one](https://www.waveshare.com/product/iot-communication/wired-comm-converter/ethernet-to-rs232-rs485/rs232-485-to-eth.htm) (please click and see the specs to see if you agree). Available working modes: TCP Server, TCP Client, UDP Server, UDP Client, HTTPD Client (supports GET and POST). I've increased the TCP Server MAX Sockets from the default 8 to the maximum of 16, but that doesn't seem to make a difference. Another thing I could try to speed things up at that side is raise the master-slaves connection from 9600 to 38400 baud.

By the way, _does_ pymodbus use more than one socket?

> 
> Actually homeassisstant do tell you exactly when which integratations start, and lately it even includes the startup time in seconds....that is a lot more than "something".

Yeah, but it didn't say "You've got a whole lotta sensors in your yaml dude, are you sure you need 'm all?" :) :).

> 
> We might consider changing modbus so that it starts fast and does the real work afterwards, right now connections need to be open and all sensors read once (initial state) before we consider modbus have started.

That sounds like a very good idea, besides the part with reading the sensors once (see below). I think the bootstrap/start-up phase should only be used by an integration to see if it's _technically_ ready. Later, when in operational phase, the integration can provide values, warnings and errors about sensors. But that's my view as a non-home-assistant software designer knowing almost nothing about HA's architecture and design thoughts, so I could be wrong. Nevertheless, I see a lot of integrations acting like that.

In the meantime I discovered the following: when I add `scan_interval: 60` to all 170 sensors, Home Assistant starts up quickly and without blocking message:

```
2023-02-01 10:48:28.200 DEBUG (SyncWorker_1) [pymodbus.client.sync] Connection to Modbus server established. Socket ('192.168.16.140', 55595)
2023-02-01 10:48:28.201 INFO (SyncWorker_1) [homeassistant.components.modbus.modbus] modbus Waveshare Meterkast communication open
```

One `scan_interval` later the first sensor is read:

```
2023-02-01 10:49:27.098 DEBUG (SyncWorker_5) [pymodbus.client.sync] New Transaction state 'SENDING'
... 168 lines of SENDING messages (I really counted them) ...
2023-02-01 10:50:11.797 DEBUG (SyncWorker_1) [pymodbus.client.sync] New Transaction state 'SENDING'
```

And right after that 170th SENDING message I see the browser window with Home Assistant reporting is has started. Now the complete start-up process of HA is done in 1 minute and 43 seconds. That's progress!

When I set the scan_interval of 10 sensors (5 per slave) to 15 seconds and leave the rest at 60 seconds, start-up is a little bit slower, I now see 200 SENDING messages (170 + 3*10, correct) before HA reports it has started. Adding more devices with more sensors and/or decreasing scan intervals could slow up things too much again.

I definitely think it is a good idea to do less work and take less time during start-up. _Maybe_ read only one sensor to see if it's technically working (without waiting for the scan interval). Reading all sensors once at start-up could still be slowing down things too much if there are many modbus devices and/or sensors. I think it might be better to postpone all sensor reading alltogether until HA has finished start-up, or at least add a configuration variable to enable that.

It would also be nice to have a `modbus: scan_interval ` option so one only has to edit the `sensor: scan_interval` of differently set sensors instead of all. The datanerd in me wants to add 12 1-phase kWh-meters alongside the two 3-phase SDM630's. That would total up to 14 slaves and about 600 sensors or so. I think I need a serious conversation with myself :).

If you would like me to do some more testing, perhaps after updating the code, I'd be happy to so please let me know.

Here is a "normal" debug log:

As you can see there are RECV lines, which mean the device responds. So I still state that in your case the device do not respond, that is also the reason for the many SEND, that is actually retries.

Of course your tcp-rs485 converter uses tcp, but be aware modbus have 2 formats that uses TCP one is called socket framer and is typically used to real modbus devices (not converters) and RTUOVERTCP which is typically used for converters.

> As you can see there are RECV lines, which mean the device responds. So I still state that in your case the device do not respond, that is also the reason for the many SEND, that is actually retries.

Aaaahhhh ... you said "run the modbus integration with debug as pr documentation" so I went to [HA's Modbus page](https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/modbus/#opening-an-issue) and copied those settings. But the RECV message are under pymodbus.transaction, not pymodbus.client ... that explains the riddle of not receiving, but still receiving. I see a lot messages like this now:

> Of course your tcp-rs485 converter uses tcp, but be aware modbus have 2 formats that uses TCP one is called socket framer and is typically used to real modbus devices (not converters) and RTUOVERTCP which is typically used for converters.

I can use both modes with this Waveshare device. During the course of this conversation, it's work mode was set to "TCP Server, ModbusTCP" which works with `modbus: type: tcp`, as you can see in the log snippet above. I also can set it's work mode to "TCP Server, None". In that case it's transparant and works when I set `modbus: type: rtuovertcp`. A really neat, versatile device!

I don't know which of the two types is preferable, so I leave it to `tcp` for now.

> Your enhancements ideas might be good, suggest them in the community and see if they get voted up.

Would be nice :). Well, things are a lot clearer now, thx for your assistance!
You need to check is there is a RECV for every SEND, if you have one without RECV, then you have the culprit.

> You need to check is there is a RECV for every SEND, if you have one without RECV, then you have the culprit.

The problem is not the communication, the problem lies in the code - or at least to a large extent. I can be wrong, but the _plural of 170_ phenomenon (see below) makes me think. Please see these two sets of files I have prepared for you:

### Start-up with scan_interval set
[yaml with the sensor definitions](https://github.com/jov58/home-assistant/blob/main/modbus/with_scaninterval.yaml)
There are 170 sensors with 10 of them having scan_interval set to 15, the others to 60.
[log output during start-up phase](https://github.com/jov58/home-assistant/blob/main/modbus/with_scaninterval.log)
There are 200 SEND and 200 RECV messages before Home Assistant reports that it has started.

Apparantly, during the start-up phase, the code already uses the scan_interval somehow because in 60 secs there are 4 x 10 + 1 x 160 = 200 readings. Can't be a coincidence. Anyway, _setting_ the scan_interval seemingly enables the code to determine that it has read all sensors and that it's ready. Or avoids the problem that it isn't.

### Start-up with no scan_interval set
[yaml with the sensor definitions](https://github.com/jov58/home-assistant/blob/main/modbus/without_scaninterval.yaml)
There are now 170 sensors with no scan_interval set.
[log output during start-up phase](https://github.com/jov58/home-assistant/blob/main/modbus/without_scaninterval.log)
There are 1392 SEND and 1388 RECV messages before Home Assistant reports that it has started.

If you look at the logs, you'll see a problem at exactly a _plural of 170_ every time. First one at transaction 170, others at 510, 680, 1020, 1190 and 1360. Transaction 340 was the lucky one I guess :). That's too much of a coincidence for me to see it as a communication problem. It seems to me that _omitting_ the scan_interval somehow brings up a problem that makes the code assume that it is not ready yet.

### Log problem
The reason why I didn't see RECV messages is also clear. After each `"[pymodbus.transaction] SEND:"` there is a `"[pymodbus.client.base] New Transaction state "SENDING""` , but after each `"[pymodbus.transaction] RECV:"` message there is no new transaction state message. To be consistent I would add that to `[pymodbus.client.base]`.
